facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: However, these are rare features on the surface of the Earth and only 190 structures are currently known and accepted as confirmed impact structures... out of which three confirmed impact structures are from India (e.g. Lonar, Dhala and Ramgarh craters).
facts.text: The Geological Survey of India recognizes Lonar as one of three confirmed terrestrial meteorite impact craters in India displaying shock metamorphism.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The Lonar crater is a relatively small (rim to rim diameter 1830 m), almost perfectly circular simple (bowl-shaped) impact crater centered at 19°58'N and 76°31'E.
facts.text: The circular Lonar crater has an average rim-to-rim diameter of approximately 1.8 kilometres.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The crater measures 1.8 km (1.1 mi) in diameter and is 150 m (490 ft) deep.
facts.text: The depth from the raised rim crest of the crater down to the crater basin floor measures approximately 150 metres.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: While earlier analyses dated the structure to 52 ± 6 ka, subsequent argon-argon dating (40Ar/39Ar) yielded a much older age of 570 ± 47 ka. However, the 40Ar/39Ar age has been disputed, as inherited argon in the samples may have resulted in an overestimation of the crater's age.
facts.source_name: Geology (Jourdan et al.) / Physical Research Laboratory
facts.text: The age of the Lonar crater impact is disputed between earlier thermoluminescence dating placing it at roughly 52,000 years ago and subsequent argon-argon geochronology dating it to roughly 570,000 years ago.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: When the meteor hit, the pressure was so intense it turned regular minerals into maskelynite (a type of glass that only forms under extreme shock pressures from a meteorite collision).
facts.text: Geological studies established the hypervelocity meteorite impact origin of the crater by detecting maskelynite, a shock-metamorphosed mineral glass formed under extreme kinetic pressures in basalt.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Lonar Lake's color shift occurred over the span of a few days. The change is visible in this image pair, acquired on May 25 and June 10 with the Operational Land Imager (OLI) on Landsat 8.
facts.text: In June 2020 CE, the water of Lonar Lake underwent an unexpected, rapid colour transformation from emerald green to bright pink within a few days.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: A localized text, the Lonar Mahatmya (or Virajakshetra Mahatmya), composed in the late 18th or early 19th century, expands the tale in eleven chapters, narrated by Vyasa to Skanda, integrating every feature of the crater into the legend...
facts.text: The Lonar Mahatmya, a regional sacred text affiliated with the Skanda Purana, identifies the crater as the subterranean lair of the demon Lonasura.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Vishnu descended in the form of a handsome youth, discovered the demon's underground dwelling with the help of his sisters, threw open the lid of his subterranean lair, and killed him within the very pit where he had resided.
facts.text: The Skanda Purana tradition relates that Lord Vishnu incarnated as the youth Daitya Sudan to uncover the demon's underground cave and slay him in his pit.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The Lonar lake is supposed to be the pit within which the giant had resided, with its water representing his blood. A nearby hill is supposed to be the lid which Vishnu had thrown open.
facts.text: Local oral legend maintains that the saline water of Lonar Lake is the demon Lonasura's spilled blood and that a nearby hill represents the subterranean stone lid cast aside by Vishnu.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Henry Cousens dates the temple to the end of the 13th and beginning of the 14th centuries CE. He is of the opinion that the construction of the temple was never completed due to invasions of the Delhi Sultanate.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India / Henry Cousens
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India protects the medieval Daitya Sudan Temple at Lonar, a Hemadpanthi-style star-shaped structure dated by archaeologist Henry Cousens to around 1300 CE.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: These mountains produce all the requisites for making glass and soap. And here are saltpetre works which yield a considerable revenue to the State, from the duties collected.
facts.text: The Mughal administrative text Ain-i-Akbari recorded in roughly 1598 CE that Lonar was an active mining and industrial site where saltpetre, glass, and soap were manufactured from its waters.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Lonar Lake. Buldhana, Maharashtra. Designated 22 July 2020. Reference no. 2441.
facts.text: Lonar Lake was officially recognized as an internationally protected wetland under the Ramsar Convention in 2020 CE.
